doc.title: "Papa Jack" Laine and Mrs. "Papa Jack" Laine Interview, 1960-05-23

chapter: La Rocca and the jazz-origin dispute
title: La Rocca's claims and Manuel Mello teaching him cornet
summary: Russell raises a Tulane article; the Laines say Mello taught La Rocca, who could barely play at first, and dispute his Tiger Rag claim.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Growl, plunger and derby: the trumpet mute tradition

blocks.x: How was Nick LaRocca in those days? Oh, brother.

Here's a big article they got out on the... Another one? That's in the Tulane paper. He gave a lot of his things to Tulane. Of course, he tells them that he's the one that started jazz. Oh. Oh, oh, my God. That's awful. Well, let them have their fun.

Let them have their fun. Listen, how... There's a magazine section there when he was a couple of years old, I don't know how much, a couple of weeks ago. He states then that he had to hide a cornet that he had in the well in his home. Yes. How could he do such a thing? When the first... He didn't even know how to hold a cornet in his mouth when he played with... He used to sit in the Elmire Pleasure Ground... Well, he did. ...in the park. And Manuel Marlowe is the man that showed him how to blow the cornet.

He used to, you know, play, but not anywhere as good, you understand? So this Manuel Marlowe, one of the leaders of my band, I had a couple of bands, of course, the leaders in all these bands. I don't get it.
How they can tell such a thing?
Well, all the time, most of all, Nick used to come with Manuel Marlowe. And Manuel Marlowe used to show him how to finger and all that stuff and break him in on these...
And he had a number of all of them. On these numbers, you understand?
Yeah. See? So, uh... That he played. Then Nick got along with playing pretty bad. As you know, with his brass band. He got along pretty good with his connet.
Hold on, that's a shame after that. Well, that's... Your wife's telling about, you said he used to play funerals?

He said he did? Yes, there was a magazine article in the paper about that. And I will be willing. I'd go stand up anyways. I'd fight him to the last. Because he is a liar. Plain-faced liar. He didn't even know how to put the connet in his mouth at that time. When he first started to play, when he used to be at Elmire Pleasure Ground with him. And after that, he used to come to the house there on Charter Street and try to rehearse them. Manuel tried to show him how to play. Then after that, he used to leave them go in the parades. Yeah. But he couldn't play though. But he went in the parades, in the carnival parades with the horn. But not that he played. Because he couldn't play. Well... I can tell him that.

Of course, he began to improve a considerable lot. Yeah. But when I'd take him in the parades, I'd pay him as well as I paid the rest of the men. So he couldn't play much then? Well, he couldn't play very much, no. In fact, whether he didn't know how to play these numbers or not, I don't know. But eventually he did. He got onto all of that stuff, you see. Then he began to play the connet pretty good. He played a pretty good trumpet.

That's another liar. That he... That Tiger Rag. He's another liar. He didn't write Tiger Rag. No, he didn't. No, not half of it, no. Because he played... And Alcide Nunes, they used to call it plurine and meatballs, the same thing. And he's the one that played it, but not La Raffin.

I'm different, putting a name from meatball, plurine, keep a shuffling and all that sort of stuff. I don't know how they can get the liars. But you can bet all he writes and all he has written and all he has said.
He never mentions him. He never mentions him. He never mentions him. Not once, does he? No, not, no. No, you bet not.
Only they'd get together and practice this stuff, you understand? Of course, you know, they'd knock out a full tune. With chorus and everything else to it.
